extracted.intended_audience: JPO patent examiners; patent applicants and their attorneys
extracted.subtask_description: Official Japan Patent Office guidance on how to conduct substantive patent examination (claim interpretation, prior art search, notices of refusal, applicant responses, interviews, outsourced searches, and examiner training). Targets examiners' decision-making and applicants' interaction with examiners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specifying claimed invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Claimed inventions should be specified based on statements in claims. Examiners take into consideration statements in the description and drawings, as well as the common general knowledge at the time of filing, in interpreting the meanings of terms used in claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even though a claim is unclear, if the claim can be clearly identified by interpreting the terms in the claim based on the description etc., examiners should specify the claimed invention, taking into consideration that interpretation. When a claim is unclear, even if the description etc. are taken into account, the examiner does not specify a claimed invention. Such a claim may be excluded from the subject of prior art search. (GL Part I, Chap. 2, Sec. 2)

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of subject of prior art search (include working examples and reasonably expected amendments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should take into consideration working examples of a claimed invention which are shown in the description as the subject of prior art searches. Also, elements which are reasonably expected to be recited in amended claims should be taken into account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventions which may be excluded from the subject of prior art search include: inventions to which new technical matter is apparently added; subject matter which is apparently patent‑ineligible; or inventions which cannot be identified even when the description is taken into consideration. Even when a claimed invention may be excluded, if it is reasonably expected, taking into account a possible amendment, that the invention can overcome the exclusion, the examiner conducts prior art searches based on a virtually amended claim. (GL Part I, Chap.2, Sec.2)

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and strategy of prior art searches
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should retrieve all prior arts relevant to claimed inventions and determine the scope of prior art searches based on their own knowledge and experience from the perspective of efficiency of the searches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should first search the technical field most probable to retrieve relevant prior arts (usually that most relevant to working examples in the description), then gradually extend to less relevant fields if needed. Where examiners cannot retrieve enough prior arts for denying novelty or inventive step in the initially searched fields, and believe it probable to retrieve such prior arts from less relevant fields, they should extend the search. Examiners may stop searches when they have retrieved enough relevant prior arts, there is little expectation of retrieving more significantly relevant prior arts, or they have retrieved a document which denies novelty or inventive step based on the document itself. When prior art information is stated in the description, examiners should consider those cited prior arts before searching for other prior arts. When search/examination results by foreign Offices or outsourced searches are available, the examiner should consider those results. (GL Part I, Chap.2, Sec.2)

rubrics_metrics.name: Retrieval and use of foreign and outsourced search results
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should consider search and/or examination results by foreign Offices and search results by outsourced prior art searches when available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When outsourcing prior art searches, dialog-based (personal meeting) report is preferred for quality and workload reduction; foreign language patent document searches can be outsourced to registered research organizations. Examiners may consider such outsourced search results in forming their examination conclusions. (GL Part I, Chap.2, Sec.2)

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison for novelty determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners specify the claimed invention and the prior art, and then compare both in determining novelty and an inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a result of the comparison, they determine that the claimed invention lacks novelty when there is no difference between claimed elements and elements specifying prior art. When there is a difference, the claimed invention is novel. (GL Part I, Chap.2, Sec.2)

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: When a difference between the claimed invention and prior art exists, examiners determine whether there is an inventive step by considering factors in support of existence/nonexistence of an inventive step based on the contents of the prior arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With regard to reasons denying an inventive step, the examiner needs to clarify the differences between the claimed invention and elements specifying prior arts, and specifically describe the reason that a person skilled in the art would easily arrive at the claimed invention based on the prior art. (GL Part I, Chap.2, Sec.2 & Sec.3)

rubrics_metrics.name: Notification of reasons for refusal (obligation and opportunity to respond)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners shall notify the applicants reasons for refusal and give the said applicants an opportunity to submit a written argument before they render a decision of refusal. (Article 50 of the Patent Act)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Types of notices include non‑final and final notices. A first-time notice about reasons in examination is non‑final. Whether a notice is non‑final or final depends on the reasons raised, not the number of notices. (GL Part I, Chap.2, Sec.3)

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and sufficiency of notice of reasons for refusal
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should prepare notifications of reasons for refusal that are clear and sufficient so that applicants can easily understand and respond to the notices. Each reason should be accompanied with the claims concerned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For inventive step refusals, examiners must clarify claim‑to‑prior‑art differences and explain why a person skilled in the art would arrive at the claimed invention. When notifying “final” reasons for refusal, examiners must explicitly indicate that the notice is “final” and the reason for such; otherwise the notice cannot be regarded as final. (GL Part I, Chap.2, Sec.3)

rubrics_metrics.name: Record of search in notifications
rubrics_metrics.description: When examiners notify reasons for refusal after conducting first‑time prior art searches, they should indicate in the notification the technical fields that they searched.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical fields should be indicated by International Patent Classifications (IPCs). If there are prior arts which do not constitute the grounds for refusal but may serve as useful references for the applicant, examiners may identify those prior arts in the notification. (GL Part I, Chap.2, Sec.2, 3.2)

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of applicants' amendments and arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants can make amendments and/or submit written arguments within the period designated in the notification. When such are filed, the examiner determines (i) whether the reasons raised in the notice are resolved, and (ii) whether any other reasons should be raised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If amendments/arguments lead the examiner to believe previous searches are insufficient, they should re‑search. Examiners are not required to conduct additional searches when they can advance examinations without them. If all reasons raised are resolved and there are no more reasons, the examiner renders a decision to grant a patent. If any reason raised is not resolved, examiners render decisions of refusal in principle, but may notify final reasons if they can indicate a possible response expected from the applicant. (GL Part I, Chap.2, Sec.4 & Sec.5)

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for further notice when new reasons arise
rubrics_metrics.description: When, although all reasons notified are resolved, the examiner finds other reasons for refusal, they send a further notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criteria for determining whether the further notice is non‑final or final: Where a new reason is raised because of an amendment made as a response to the last notice, the further notice should be final. On the other hand, where a new reason should have been raised in the last notice (but was not raised), the further notice should be non‑final. (GL Part I, Chap.2, Sec.3)

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments allowed after final notice of reasons for refusal (limitations)
rubrics_metrics.description: After the final notice of reasons for refusal, the applicant may amend the claims for limited purposes: deleting claims; restricting the scope of claimed inventions in a limited way; correcting errors; or clarifying ambiguous statements on which an objection that the statements are unclear was raised (Japanese Patent Act Art. 17bis(5)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This restriction is provided for the efficiency of examinations and violating it does not constitute grounds for invalidation. In applying the provision, the examiner should ensure, giving due consideration to the objective thereof, that it should not be applied more strictly than necessary—especially when the examiner believes that the results of the examination already performed can be used effectively to complete the examination process promptly even if an amendment does not comply with the restriction. (GL Part IV, Chap.4)

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision to grant or refuse (what must be described)
rubrics_metrics.description: When deciding refusal, examiners need to determine whether the reasons notified are resolved or not, and whether the reasons notified are appropriate or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the decision of refusal, all reasons which are not resolved should be described. Each reason should be clearly described and be accompanied with the claims concerned. Examiners should also describe their determinations on issues raised in written arguments. (GL Part I, Chap.2, Sec.5)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of interviews to improve examination quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Examination by interview is implemented to improve accuracy of examination, smooth communication with applicants, allow the examiner to appropriately understand important points of the application, and assist with draft amendments and suggestions for amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an examiner is already assigned, the applicant requests interview with that examiner. If an applicant or attorney requests an interview, the examiner accepts at least one interview in principle. If an applicant appoints an attorney, the interview is between attorney and examiner; the applicant or authorized staff may attend. Interviews may be held from the date a request for examination is filed to the date a patent right is granted. During the period when an applicant may file an appeal, if an interview is requested before filing the appeal the applicant must present a concrete reason for the appeal and a draft amendment. Purposes include explaining technological characteristics, comparing invention with prior art, and explaining draft amendments; supplemental materials may be used. (Implementation, requirements, period, and purpose sections)

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiners' objectives in interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: From the examiner’s viewpoint, interviews must enable the examiner to understand technological characteristics (important constituents, effects), what portion of the description the applicant seeks patent for, and how prior art comparisons affect patentability and amendment effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Information from interviews is used to determine examination policy before starting examinations (e.g., how searches should be performed), to confirm understanding of prior art cited by applicant or examiner, to confirm what in the detailed description corresponds to amendment constituents, and to confirm whether a draft amendment can eliminate the reason for refusal. (Sections on purpose from examiner’s viewpoint)

rubrics_metrics.name: Video interview system and technical provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Videoconferencing is an available option to conduct examination interviews, making it easier for distant applicants to participate and improving interaction and accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No special software is necessary; participants need a computer, webcam, headset, and facsimile. The system supports up to 10 locations, displays video images of participants, supports uploading documents (Word/Excel/PowerPoint/PDF), whiteboard annotation, pointer, and chat for URLs and text. (Video interview & system sections)

rubrics_metrics.name: Outsourcing prior art searches to registered research organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: JPO examiners outsource preliminary prior art searches to registered research organizations to improve efficiency; the searcher reports results to the examiner, preferably via dialog-based personal meeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two delivery methods: dialog‑based (personal meeting) and report‑based; dialog‑based accounted for about 98% of outsourced searches (FY2014). To improve quality, foreign patent document searches are outsourced as well (about 52% were foreign document searches in FY2014). Number of registered organizations grew from one in 2004 to eleven in 2014. (Outsourced prior art searches section)

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner qualification and training roadmap
rubrics_metrics.description: The JPO trains new recruits with diverse backgrounds so they become qualified examiners in 2–4 years through on‑ and off‑the‑job training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training includes Assistant examiner course, Examiner course Part I and II, OJT Phase 1 and 2, visualization of OJT (e.g., check sheet). OJT Phase 1: put knowledge into practice and acquire fundamental examination practices; OJT Phase 2 (3–5th year): check practical skills, acquire broader view and practical skills mainly on examination practices other than fundamental ones, promoted to an Examiner with full discretion when qualified. (HRD and roadmap sections)
